title: Colostomy Care
path: Nursing Care of Patients with Feeding and Elimination Problems

headings.title: Introduction and Indications for Colostomy
headings.content: A colostomy is a surgical procedure that brings a portion of the colon through the abdominal wall to create a stoma, serving as an alternative route for waste elimination. Nursing students in Nigeria must understand that this procedure is performed when a section of the large intestine or rectum needs to be bypassed or removed due to various pathological conditions. Common indications include colorectal cancer, severe diverticulitis, inflammatory bowel disease such as Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, bowel ischemia, trauma, and congenital anomalies like Hirschsprung's disease in pediatric patients. Colostomies can be temporary, allowing distal bowel to heal following surgery or trauma, or permanent, when the rectum and lower colon are completely removed or must be permanently bypassed. As future nurses, recognizing these indications helps contextualize patient anxiety and guides comprehensive preoperative and postoperative planning. Understanding the underlying pathology also aids the nurse in anticipating the patient's specific care needs, expected stoma function, and emotional support requirements during hospital admission and subsequent community reintegration in the Nigerian healthcare setting.

headings.title: Types of Colostomies and Anatomical Considerations
headings.content: The anatomical location of a colostomy dictates the consistency of the stool output and specific management strategies, which is vital clinical knowledge for nursing practice. Colostomies are classified by their anatomical site on the large intestine: ascending, transverse, descending, and sigmoid colostomies. An ascending colostomy is located on the right side of the abdomen; the stool output is typically liquid to semi-liquid and contains high digestive enzyme content, posing a severe risk of skin breakdown. A transverse colostomy, often created in an emergency, is located in the upper abdomen and usually produces semi-formed to loose stool. Descending and sigmoid colostomies are situated on the left side of the abdomen, yielding firmer, more formed stool because much of the water has been reabsorbed as waste travels through the length of the colon. Sigmoid colostomies are the most common type of permanent colostomy, often resulting from abdominoperineal resection for rectal cancer. In addition to anatomical location, colostomies are categorized by construction type: end stomas, loop stomas (which have both a proximal functioning opening and a distal non-functioning opening), and double-barrel stomas. Recognizing these anatomical differences helps nurses anticipate stool consistency, select appropriate pouching systems, and accurately educate patients on what to expect postoperatively.

headings.title: Preoperative and Postoperative Nursing Assessment
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing assessment is critical across both preoperative and postoperative phases for a patient undergoing colostomy surgery. Preoperatively, the nurse assesses the patient's baseline physical status, nutritional condition, psychological readiness, and understanding of the procedure. A crucial preoperative responsibility is stoma site marking, usually performed by an enterostomal therapist or trained nurse with the patient in sitting, standing, and lying positions to ensure the stoma is visible to the patient, avoids skin folds, scars, and the beltline, and allows proper appliance adherence. Postoperatively, the nurse conducts frequent systematic evaluations. This includes monitoring vital signs for hemorrhage or shock, assessing abdominal wound dressings, and evaluating bowel function return through the presence of bowel sounds or the passage of flatus and stool through the stoma. The nurse must also monitor fluid and electrolyte balance, especially with high-output stomas, and assess the patient's psychological adaptation to body image changes. Pain management is paramount to encourage early ambulation, which prevents postoperative complications such as deep vein thrombosis and paralytic ileus. Documenting baseline color, size, and output of the stoma provides an essential comparison point to detect early complications.

headings.title: Stoma and Peristomal Skin Assessment
headings.content: Evaluating the health of the stoma and the surrounding peristomal skin is a fundamental nursing competency in stoma care. A healthy stoma should appear moist, shiny, and pink to deep red in color, mirroring the color of the oral mucous membrane. This rich vascularity makes the stoma prone to minor bleeding when cleaned, which is considered normal. Immediately postoperatively, mild edema (swelling) is expected, but this should subside over the first six to eight weeks. The nurse must measure the stoma size accurately with each pouch change, as the stoma shrinks during the initial weeks. Conversely, a pale, dusky, cyanotic, or black stoma indicates compromised blood supply, ischemia, or necrosis, which requires immediate surgical notification. Peristomal skin assessment is equally vital; the skin surrounding the stoma must remain intact, dry, and free from redness, excoriation, or fungal rashes. Any leakage of effluent onto the skin causes chemical irritation and breakdown. Nurses must inspect the peristomal area during every appliance change, looking for signs of contact dermatitis, candidiasis, or mechanical trauma caused by improper pouch removal techniques, ensuring timely intervention and barrier cream application when indicated.

headings.title: Colostomy Appliance Selection and Pouching Technique
headings.content: Selecting the correct colostomy appliance and mastering the pouching technique are essential for preventing complications and maintaining the patient's quality of life. Appliances can be one-piece systems (where the skin barrier and pouch are integrated) or two-piece systems (where the skin barrier remains on the skin and the pouch snaps or locks on separately). The choice depends on patient dexterity, visual acuity, lifestyle, and stoma characteristics. When performing a pouching change, the nurse or patient gently removes the old appliance from top to bottom while pushing the skin away, cleans the peristomal skin with warm water and mild, residue-free soap, and pats the area completely dry. The nurse measures the stoma and traces the exact size and shape onto the back of the skin barrier, cutting an opening approximately 1/8 to 1/4 inch larger than the stoma to prevent trauma while avoiding exposed skin. Skin barriers, protective powders, or skin sealants may be applied to protect raw or weeping skin. The new pouch is centered over the stoma, pressed firmly from the bottom up to ensure a secure seal, and closed securely at the tail end. Proper application prevents effluent leakage, protects the peristomal skin, and instills confidence in the recovering patient.

headings.title: Patient Education and Self-Care Management
headings.content: Patient education and self-care management are central pillars of nursing care, empowering individuals to regain independence after colostomy surgery. Education must begin preoperatively and continue throughout the hospital stay, incorporating family members or caregivers when appropriate. The nurse teaches the patient how to empty the pouch when it is one-third to one-half full, how to change the entire appliance system, and how to recognize the signs of normal stoma function versus complications. It is vital to address psychological aspects, as body image disturbance, anxiety, and social isolation are common challenges. Nurses should encourage patients to express their feelings, introduce them to support groups or peer visitors, and reassure them that modern appliances are discreet, odor-proof, and allow for normal clothing choices and activities. In the Nigerian context, culturally sensitive counseling is crucial to address community stigmas, dietary customs, and religious practices related to bodily elimination. Before discharge, the nurse must ensure the patient or caregiver demonstrates competent stoma care skills, knows where to procure supplies locally, and has a scheduled follow-up appointment with a healthcare provider or enterostomal nurse.

headings.title: Nutritional Considerations and Dietary Guidelines
headings.content: Nutritional considerations and dietary guidelines play a significant role in managing stool consistency and minimizing bothersome stoma symptoms such as excessive gas, odor, and blockage. Immediately following surgery, patients typically progress from clear liquids to a regular diet as bowel motility returns. For patients with colostomies—especially descending or sigmoid colostomies—a varied diet is generally well-tolerated, but certain foods require individual modification. Nurses must educate patients on identifying foods that cause gas and odor, such as beans, cabbage, onions, garlic, eggs, and carbonated beverages. Foods that may cause stoma blockage, particularly in patients with high-output or loop stomas, include nuts, corn, popcorn, raw celery, and fibrous fruits with skins; thorough chewing is heavily emphasized. Adequate hydration is essential, but patients should be advised that drinking fluids with meals may increase stoma output speed. In Nigeria, where diets often feature high-fiber local foods, yams, beans, and vegetables, nurses must guide patients on how to introduce these traditional meals gradually while monitoring their individual gastrointestinal responses and maintaining adequate fluid intake to prevent dehydration.

headings.title: Identifying and Managing Colostomy Complications
headings.content: Identifying and managing colostomy complications promptly is essential for preventing long-term morbidity and ensuring patient safety. Common early complications include stoma ischemia or necrosis resulting from tension or compromised blood supply, peristomal skin breakdown caused by chemical irritation from effluent leakage, mucocutaneous separation where the stoma detaches from the skin, and minor stoma bleeding. Late complications include stoma retraction (where the stoma pulls below the skin level), prolapse (excessive protrusion of the bowel through the stoma site), parastomal hernia (weakening of the abdominal musculature around the stoma site), and bowel obstruction or stenosis (narrowing of the stoma lumen). Nursing responsibilities involve regular inspection, prompt reporting of abnormal findings to the surgeon, providing skin barrier adjustments, applying specialized pastes or powders, and teaching patients how to identify red-flag symptoms such as severe abdominal pain, high fever, persistent nausea and vomiting, or sudden cessation of stool output. Early nursing intervention and referral to an enterostomal therapist can resolve many minor issues before they require major surgical revision.
